articles.title: 'If you want an RTX 5080 better buy one while you can still afford one': as Nvidia's RTX 5090 reportedly disappears, gamers are worried about more price hikes — and I'm concerned about the entire future of GeForce GPUs
articles.text:
Are we seeing the first signs of Nvidia abandoning PC gamers? As the RTX 5090 seemingly disappears from shelves, I'm getting more worried about GeForce GPUs
Ge-Forced out by AI and cloud gaming?
It's been a theory for quite some time now that Nvidia is — what's the polite way to put this? — let's say deprioritizing PC gamers, perhaps, or more specifically, its gaming graphics cards. But this week has added more evidence to the collective weight that GeForce GPUs are increasingly at risk of being sidelined further by Team Green.
I'm talking first about the story that emerged a few days ago, where a leaker claimed Nvidia is diverting all GB202 (Blackwell) chips to make AI (RTX Pro) graphics cards. That's the graphics processor used in the RTX 5090, but apparently not anymore; it's for AI boards only now, we're told.
That makes some sense as the RTX 5090 is already disappearing from shelves, certainly in the US, where you can't buy one for less than the best part of 10 grand (from gouging third-party sellers, with no major retailers actually having stock anymore). So arguably this effective discontinuation of the RTX 5090 is already happening.
On top of that, the latest developments are that Micro Center is reportedly listing the Blackwell flagship as 'not carried', and Nvidia itself has removed all mention of the RTX 5090 from its own GPU marketplace (though it is still mentioned elsewhere on the site). Search for the RTX 5090 on that marketplace, and you won't find it any longer — the highest-end graphics card listed is now the RTX 5080 (hat tip to Wccftech for spotting this being flagged up on Reddit).
Aside from an actual announcement from Nvidia (which probably wouldn't ever happen anyway), that seems like about as clear an indication you can get that the RTX 5090 has been shoved out of the exit door, never to return, because Nvidia needs those GB202 chips where they are most profitable. RTX Pro GPUs offer a much heftier premium that Team Green can heap on top.
A new Blackwell flagship?
So, what does this mean? For starters, if it is true that the RTX 5090 has been scrapped, the RTX 5080 becomes the flagship Nvidia GeForce GPU. Once the existing stock of RTX 5090s has been depleted, this could mean the price of the RTX 5080 is inflated. When I say inflated, I mean jacked up even more, because it has already seen some nasty price hikes. Currently, the RTX 5080 is at around $1,800 in the US on Newegg, or £1,450 on Overclockers in the UK – and those are the lowest prices; it goes up from there. It's a very similar story in many other regions.
This is clearly a concern for gamers as you can see from the Reddit thread I pointed out above, with comments such as: "If you want a 5080 better buy one while you can still afford one." Really, it's debatable if the card is anything like 'affordable' relative to its graphical frame rate muscle even now.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Here's where another rumor comes into play. Elsewhere on the grapevine, there's talk that Nvidia may actually release the RTX 5080 Super variant which has long been speculated about. This would be a 24GB graphics card, and it'd essentially replace the discontinued RTX 5090 – with the theory being that Nvidia would also ditch the vanilla RTX 5080 (16GB). This would leave the rumored RTX 5080 Super as the sole high-end GeForce graphics card, quite some distance above the RTX 5070 Ti.
If that happens, imagine the pricing concerns here – what MSRP would Nvidia attach to the RTX 5080 Super? And then consider the cost inflation that will be added when you take into account that this card will also be sought after for AI usage (as seen with the RTX 5090).
If an RTX 5080 Super is indeed inbound for early 2027, that would also suggest that the next-gen RTX 6000 family is further away than some rumors believe – as this Super version would be a stopgap GPU to keep the Blackwell range ticking over. The RAM crisis may have a fair bit to do with this strategy also, given that most predictions foresee it getting worse next year (and the misery continuing into 2028, and maybe beyond). Of course, launching a new GeForce range into such memory headwinds wouldn't be easy.
Software focus and streaming dreams
All in all, it feels to me like there's a stream of subtle – and not so subtle – hints and rumors that Nvidia is very much slowing down the development of gaming GPUs (while not wanting to give that impression, naturally). The other part of the equation here is the increased focus on the software side, of course, rather than the hardware. DLSS 5 is out and Nvidia is already pushing hard with honing and refining that neural rendering tech, and something else that happened earlier this week was that Team Green highlighted some big leaps in performance here. Pretty huge strides forward, in fact.
Of course, you could argue that all the development resources being ploughed into DLSS – including frame generation, which got a hefty boost alongside DLSS 5 – shows Nvidia isn't abandoning gaming GPUs for PC gamers. And I concede that's true to an extent, but there is very much a vibe of a major slowdown leading towards the feared deprioritization of GeForce GPUs – and there's another angle to consider here too: cloud gaming.
Don't forget that GeForce Now also benefits from DLSS. Just this week, Nvidia added DLSS 4.5 override controls to the streaming service to help push up frame rates – those on the RTX 5080 (Ultimate) plan can use Dynamic Multi Frame Generation of up to 4x now. Ray Reconstruction for bolstering ray-traced visuals is available, too, among other options.
Would Nvidia rather have you subscribed to its cloud gaming service, making monthly payments, than buying a GeForce GPU for a one-off sum? It seems an obvious direction for the company to be heading in, and with increasing warning signs around Team Green's gaming GPUs, I'm becoming more convinced that this is where Nvidia's priorities are shifting for the future of PC gaming.
This isn't to say GeForce graphics cards are definitely on their way out, or that an RTX 6000 line-up won't happen – it's already well underway after all – but beyond the next generation, I'm increasingly dubious about where GeForce GPUs might fit into the big PC gaming picture. Between AI demand and cloud gaming (plus increasingly faster internet connections), there's a squeeze underway that could prove painful for the GeForce line-up – and the ongoing RAM crisis is hardly helping, either.

articles.title: BYD voit les choses en (très) grand, sa nouvelle voiture électrique fait exploser la taille des écrans
articles.text:
Le nouveau BYD Tang pousse toujours plus loin la numérisation de l’habitacle. De quoi impressionner, mais aussi relancer une question : dans nos voitures, les écrans ne sont-ils pas en train de prendre un peu trop de place ?
Vous vous rappelez quand on jugeait une voiture à son look, à son moteur, à ses équipements, au confort de ses sièges… Aujourd’hui, la taille de son écran central semble presque devenue un argument de vente à part entière, et à ce petit jeu, les constructeurs chinois n’ont clairement pas l’intention de rester spectateurs. Le téléphone au volant est interdit pour des raisons évidentes de sécurité, mais à voir ces écrans toujours plus imposants envahir nos habitacles, on peut s’interroger sur la cohérence de cette course au gigantisme…
BYD transforme son tableau de bord en écran géant
Avec la troisième génération de son SUV électrique Tang, BYD en remet une couche comme le rapporte CarNewsChina. Le constructeur dévoile une interface baptisée « Giant Screen UI », pensée pour exploiter un habitacle dominé par deux immenses dalles numériques. De quoi donner un sérieux coup de vieux à certains tableaux de bord pourtant encore récents.
Le nouveau Tang associe un affichage de 35,4", installé sous la base du pare-brise, à un écran panoramique tactile de 30" qui s’étend quant à lui sur les zones centrale et passager du tableau de bord. Le premier regroupe notamment les informations de conduite ou encore la navigation, tandis que le second se charge du multimédia et des commandes numériques.
Force est d'admettre que l'ensemble évoque davantage un poste de pilotage d’un vaisseau de science-fiction qu’un habitacle automobile. Une impression que BYD assume d'ailleurs pleinement.
Mais en voiture comme ailleurs, il n'y a pas que la taille qui compte. La nouvelle interface BYD permet ainsi de redimensionner, déplacer ou encore juxtaposer différentes fenêtres pour afficher simultanément navigation, musique et informations du véhicule. L’objectif est de rendre cet immense espace numérique toujours plus flexible, plutôt que de simplement démultiplier les pixels.
Des écrans partout, mais pour quel usage ?
BYD ajoute également un compagnon virtuel animé, baptisé Xiao Mianbao, capable de réagir grâce à la voix et à la perception visuelle. Une touche supplémentaire de technologie et d'IA, même si l’on peut s’interroger là encore sur la réelle utilité quotidienne d’un tel assistant.
Avant l'été, c'est Mercedes qui dévoilait son immense planche de bord numérique, baptisée MBUX Hyperscreen, à bord de la nouvelle Classe C, avec une dalle interminable de 99 cm.
Mais faut-il vraiment transformer chaque centimètre du tableau de bord en surface numérique ? Bien sûr, un grand écran peut améliorer la lisibilité et faciliter l’accès à certaines fonctions, mais il peut aussi concentrer trop de commandes dans des menus et se montrer très distractif, là où un ancestral bouton physique reste parfois plus rapide à utiliser, et sans avoir à quitter la route des yeux.
Et vous, que pensez-vous des écrans géants à bord ?

articles.title: iPhone Duo se revende por hasta 5.000 dólares antes de su lanzamiento: el riesgo de pagar sobreprecios
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo de Apple ya se ofrece en reventa por hasta 5.000 dólares, aunque el precio oficial de esa configuración es de 3.199 dólares. La diferencia de 1.801 dólares refleja la presión que generó el rápido agotamiento de las reservas del nuevo teléfono plegable. Por ahora, Apple no tiene disponibilidad inmediata en su tienda en línea y los pedidos directos muestran fechas de entrega para el próximo año.
Un anuncio completado en eBay registró la venta de un iPhone Duo de 2 TB en color Night Sky por 5.000 dólares. Vadim Yuryev, responsable del canal de YouTube Max Tech, fue quien señaló la operación en X. El registro corresponde a una unidad cuya configuración Apple vende en Estados Unidos por 3.199 dólares.
También se reportó la venta de una reserva confirmada del modelo de 1 TB, igualmente en color Night Sky, por 4.400 dólares. Esa versión cuesta 2.599 dólares en la tienda de Apple. En ambos casos, el comprador pagó cerca de 1.800 dólares adicionales frente al precio oficial.
Apple vende el iPhone Duo por menos, pero no tiene unidades disponibles
La diferencia entre el precio de Apple y las cifras de eBay es central para quienes consideran comprar el dispositivo ahora. La compañía ofrece el modelo de 2 TB por 3.199 dólares y el de 1 TB por 2.599 dólares, pero las reservas iniciales se agotaron poco después de que comenzaran los pedidos.
Las preventas arrancaron el viernes a las 8:00 a. m., hora del Este de Estados Unidos. En menos de cinco minutos, las fechas de entrega para todos los colores y capacidades pasaron del lanzamiento previsto para el 23 de octubre a mediados de noviembre. Media hora después, los modelos disponibles en el país indicaban entregas para el 25 de enero; algunos compradores llegaron a ver estimaciones del 29 de enero.
Las tiendas físicas de Apple también se quedaron sin las unidades previstas para el día de lanzamiento. En paralelo, decenas de dispositivos reservados aparecieron en eBay, con vendedores que llegaron a pedir hasta 5.200 dólares. Estos son precios solicitados o registrados en anuncios, y no garantizan que cada publicación se concrete en una venta.
La escasez impulsa el mercado de reventa
La disponibilidad limitada parece haber alimentado el interés por las unidades de reventa. Counterpoint Research prevé que Apple venderá alrededor de 6 millones de iPhone Duo este año, en un mercado de teléfonos plegables que todavía representa un segmento de nicho.
La fabricación de estos dispositivos puede ser más compleja que la de un teléfono convencional. El diseño requiere bisagras especializadas y pantallas flexibles, componentes que plantean desafíos de producción. El periodista tecnológico Raymond Wong ha señalado que los rendimientos de fabricación suelen ser menores que los de los smartphones tradicionales. Esa dificultad podría limitar cuántas unidades llegan al mercado mientras la producción aumenta.
También circularon reportes sobre posibles problemas de fabricación. Uno publicado en septiembre sostuvo que poco más del 60 % de las unidades ensambladas cumplía con los estándares de Apple; otro indicó que la producción diaria era de unos cientos de equipos durante la fase inicial. Apple no ha confirmado esas cifras, por lo que deben considerarse estimaciones atribuidas a informes externos.
Qué considerar antes de pagar un sobreprecio
Quien compre mediante una plataforma de reventa puede terminar pagando mucho más que el precio establecido por Apple, incluso antes de tener el equipo en sus manos. En el caso de las reservas, además, es importante verificar qué incluye la operación, cuándo se entregaría el teléfono y qué protección ofrece la plataforma si el vendedor no cumple.
La reventa puede ofrecer acceso anticipado cuando no hay existencias oficiales, pero el sobreprecio no garantiza una entrega más rápida ni elimina los riesgos de la transacción. Mientras Apple mantenga agotadas las reservas iniciales, la diferencia entre su precio y el de revendedores seguirá siendo un dato clave para evaluar si conviene esperar a que se reponga el stock.

articles.title: PowerColor Radeon RX 9050 8 Go low profile en fuite, une première du genre
articles.text:
En l'espace de quelques semaines, deux fabricants lancent des Radeon RX 9000 dites low profile. NVIDIA n'est donc plus seul sur ce segment.
Le fabricant PowerColor semble emboîter le pas de Vastarmor en annonçant une seconde carte graphique low profile, à destination des plus petites configurations. Attention cependant, il ne s'agit cette fois que d'une Radeon RX 9050, sensiblement moins puissante donc.
Blackwell/RDNA 4 se convertissent au low profile
Alors que les prix de nombreux composants sont au plus haut, plusieurs constructeurs tentent de nouvelles approches pour convaincre les acheteurs. Le succès des mini-PC s'inscrit dans cette stratégie, mais leurs performances graphiques sont souvent à la traîne.
Certaines machines compactes à base de carte mère mini-ITX ont pourtant tout ce qu'il faut côté interface pour brancher une véritable carte graphique dédiée. Problème, dans la majorité des cas, l'espace disponible est trop réduit, les cartes graphiques traditionnelles trop hautes.
Initialement prévues pour s'intégrer à des serveurs, les cartes graphiques dites « low profile » peuvent cependant constituer une alternative intéressante. Ces cartes sont aussi dites « demi-hauteur », un terme plus clair dans la langue de Molière : elles occupent moins d'espace en hauteur et peuvent donc rentrer dans des modèles de boîtiers plus compacts.
Les cartes low profile ne sont pas une nouveauté chez NVIDIA et même la toute dernière génération de GPU de la firme de Jensen Huang dispose de modèles à ce format. Que ce soit ASUS ou Gigabyte par exemple, les partenaires de NVIDIA distribuent des GeForce RTX 5060 low profile. C'est hélas moins vrai chez AMD.
Après la RX 9060 XT, une RX 9050
Une première surprise – et bonne nouvelle du même coup – est arrivée il y a seulement quelques semaines quand le YouTubeur ETA Prime a pu mettre la main sur une carte conçue par le Chinois Vastarmor.
Il s'agissait alors d'une Radeon RX 9060 XT low profile très similaire à la Radeon RX 9060 XT classique avec ses 32 unités de calcul, ses 16 Go de mémoire GDDR6 et une fréquence maximale de 3 040 MHz. La principale différence résidait dans un TGP réduit de 160 à 140 W afin de coller au système de refroidissement forcément moins performant.
Aujourd'hui, nous avons en quelque sorte une petite sœur à cette carte puisque la firme Powercolor annonce cette fois une Radeon RX 9050 au format low profile. Elle ne dispose que de 16 unités de calcul pour 1 024 processeurs de flux et le GPU est associé à 8 Go de GDDR6 sur bus 128-bit. C'est en tout point identique à une Radeon RX 9050 « classique ».
D'ailleurs, contrairement à ce qu'a été obligé de faire Vastarmor sur sa 9060, il n'est pas ici question de modifier le TGP : Powercolor conserve les 92 W officiels communiqués par AMD pour sa Radeon RX 9050. Forcément, elle sera en revanche plus compacte, mais pas non plus minuscule : on parle de 20 cm de long et de deux emplacements PCIe occupés.
Nous n'en savons hélas pas beaucoup plus et n'avons par exemple pas encore de précisions sur la date exacte de sortie envisagée par Powercolor. Nous ne savons pas non plus quelles régions du monde seront concernées ou quel sera le prix de cette petite graphique. Reste que cela offre une option de plus pour monter une machine compacte et ça, c'est toujours une bonne nouvelle.
Source : VideoCardz

articles.title: Vous pensiez que votre téléphone vous écoutait mais la vérité est bien plus ingénieuse
articles.text:
Pourquoi votre smartphone connaît vos envies sans enregistrer vos conversations
Vous pensez que votre smartphone écoute vos conversations privées pour vous afficher des publicités ciblées ? La réalité est bien différente, mais cela ne rend pas la chose plus aisée à accepter.
Damned, après une conversation avec un(e) ami(e) au sujet d’un produit, voyage ou lieu, une publicité correspondante apparaît sur votre écran. Une situation qui nous a tous fait croire au moins une fois que notre précieux smartphone nous écoute grâce à ses micros afin d’afficher ultérieurement de la pub ciblée. Cette théorie est cependant fausse, les géants de la tech préférant jouer avec une technique bien plus ingénieuse. Tadaaa ! Voici le croisement des données.
Publicité ciblée : comment les algorithmes devinent vos envies sans utiliser de micro
Contrairement à la croyance populaire, enregistrer et analyser des millions de conversations audio en temps réel n’est pas du tout ce que fait votre smartphone Android ou iOS pour vous afficher des réclames ad hoc. En plus d’exiger une puissance de calcul et des capacités de stockage colossales, cela ferait fondre la batterie de votre appareil à vue d’œil à cause des micros et l’envoi de données en continu. Dans la vraie vie, Google et Apple n’ont pas besoin de vous écouter, juste de recouper vos données avec celles de vos proches.
En toute discrétion, les algorithmes font en effet des suppositions en croisant ces informations. Si vous abordez un sujet avec un proche, l’un de vous s’est sûrement déjà renseigné dessus en ligne. Et si vos téléphones se connectent au même réseau wifi, ou que le suivi de localisation vous place physiquement au même endroit, les régies publicitaires établissent immédiatement un lien entre vos profils.
Ainsi, si votre interlocuteur consulte des articles sur le camping avant ou pendant qu’il est avec vous, le système déduit que vous en avez probablement parlé et que ce sujet pourrait vous intéresser. Il vous proposera alors des publicités ciblées dans les minutes qui suivent.
Apple iPhone 18 Pro
Collecte de données : ce que votre smartphone sait vraiment sur vous en coulisses
La quantité de données collectées en arrière-plan dépasse largement le simple cadre du navigateur internet. Chaque app que vous installez agit comme un mouchard invisible. Votre smartphone connaît votre position géographique exacte, la vitesse à laquelle vous vous déplacez, le niveau de votre batterie, et même l’inclinaison de votre terminal. Il sait à quelle heure vous vous réveillez et avec qui vous passez le plus de temps.
Ces métadonnées sont souvent agrégées et revendues par des courtiers en données, les fameux data brokers. Les apps intègrent des traqueurs invisibles qui siphonnent ces éléments pour enrichir un profil publicitaire global (si vous leur en donnez l’autorisation, évidemment).
Finalement, votre microphone reste éteint, mais votre téléphone bavarde constamment avec des dizaines de serveurs. Il vous cible ainsi à la perfection, parvenant à anticiper vos désirs avant même que vous ne les formuliez à voix haute.

articles.title: The Lenovo Yoga Pro 7i Gen 11 is a creative powerhouse with no compromises
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Yoga Pro 7i Aura Edition is a 15-inch version of the Pro 99AE Gen. It may only be about an inch less in screen real estate, but when traveling and when putting things in a bag or moving from place to place, that 1 inch of screen real estate can actually make a huge difference in portability (with fitting in a backpack or even on a small cafe table). If you plan to carry your laptop every day, whether in a backpack or on its own, this 7i is probably a good fit. If you plan to leave your laptop at your desk and want a bit more power and a bit more screen, the 9i is probably the right choice.
Reasons to buy
- + Built for mobile creators
- + Beautiful 2.5K 165Hz OLED
- + RTX 5060 GPU
- + Incredibly fast 165Hz
- + Great ports
Reasons to avoid
- - May just be worth jumping to the Pro 9i
- - Not a 4K screen
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
This is a laptop that's designed for creators who are on the go. The 15-inch screen is big enough to give you enough workspace to do what you need on the go, without being so cumbersome that it won't fit in a standard laptop backpack. 15 inches is usually the sweet spot that makes or breaks whether it fits in a standard bag.
While this may not have full 4K, it has a crisp, color-accurate display, making it fantastic for those who need absolute perfection in color profiles. It is also powerful enough to handle almost anything you throw at it. While it's not designed for the average business user, those who dabble in creative work but still need to get business done can do so with ease on this laptop.
It has enough dedicated GPU to carve through video, enough RAM to run several lines at once, a beautiful enough screen to edit photos without a problem, and a solid enough machine to handle everything else, all in one device.
In short, if you want to get this kind of work done while still on the go, this is the machine for you. If you plan to park it at a desk or workstation most of the time, the 9i may be a better fit. Either way, this is for the creator.
Lenovo Yoga Pro 7i: Price and Availability
The Lenovo Pro 7i Gen 11 Aura Edition is available direct from Lenovo in the US, in the UK, and other territories. Prices start at $2,599.99 / £2,430 for the base configuration.
My review unit, however, had a slight upgrade and was sitting around $2,700. The Yoga Pro 7 could be configured up to a Core Ultra 9 with an RTX 570, 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of SSD.
Compared to the Lenovo Yoga Pro 9i Gen 11 Aura Edition I just reviewed, which sits around $3,000 for the same configuration, the Pro 7i saves about $250 for the same CPU, GPU, RAM, and SSD storage.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
That means it is up to you whether it's worth saving $250 for giving up an inch of screen, or perhaps gaining an inch of screen for portability, depending on which camp you're in
Lenovo Yoga Pro 7i: Unboxing and First Impressions
I'll admit it, life has gotten crazy. I've had this laptop in my queue, sitting on my testing desk or in testing, for 178 days.
I've used it for: numerous meetings, a few days in my life to see how it operates, several articles have been written on it, a lot of testing, some benchmarking, thrown in the backpack a couple of times, used it as my main machine while in my home office for a couple of days
All around, this machine runs fantastic. The Luna Gray color is fantastic. It boots quickly, and it runs fast. The 15-inch OLED touchscreen is spectacular and accurate. The colors are incredible, and the ports are great. Overall, it's a laptop most people would dream of having.
I even prefer the 15-inch over the larger 16-inch 9i I just finished testing, though it is still a tad large for my liking. 14-inch seems to be my sweet spot. The 15-inch is still manageable and fits in most full-size laptop backpacks. For example, it fits well in my Nomatic Navigator and my Nomatic backpack.
Lenovo Yoga Pro 7i: Design and Build Quality
As expected, the keyboard and trackpad are spectacular. Like the 9i variant, the trackpad also doubles as a drawing surface for the Yoga Pen. Since I adjusted on the 9i, it was much easier for me to get used to it. However, as I said in the 9i review, if this is your first time using a drawing surface like this, it will take a second to get used to. It's not quite as seamless as drawing on the screen, but it becomes fairly intuitive after a little use.
The 15-inch 2.5K display is hard to recognize as only 2.5K. It looks significantly nicer than that. It could be because of the colors and the 165 Hz refresh rate, but this display (HDR True Black 1000, 100% sRGB, P3, Adobe RGB, 1,100 nits peak brightness, and PureSight) makes this OLED panel look absolutely spectacular. Unless you know for a fact you need a 4K display, you can use this for creative content pretty easily.
The last thing I'll mention is that the port layout is also what I would hope for. I've never been a fan of laptops that shove ports on the back and make it seem like they're meant to stay stationary on a desk. Even though I love the thinner laptops, I've never been a fan of the laptops that only have USB-C. I get it, and I get what they're going for, but in the professional space, that's really hard to justify.
For ultrabooks, that makes sense, but for professional business laptops or even creative laptops like this one, having only a USB-C means that you are guaranteed to need a dongle. This laptop, though, has a good range of ports for its intended use, and it's designed for that use case, which is ultimately what a laptop should be tested against anyway.
Lenovo Yoga Pro 7i: In use
I've been able to do some light photo editing and some video editing, and more, on this machine. While creating, I actually did a lot of content approval on this laptop during my testing. My roles in other companies have shifted. For now, I review content my team makes daily, so I appreciate this screen more and more.
The OLED is absolutely spectacular and has made me want an OLED panel for pretty much everything that I have. 165 Hz is also buttery smooth. The RTX 5060 is absurdly powerful. I tested it by running 22 lines of a security system I was setting up for a client without any issues. It barely taxed the memory, and I ran all 22 lines at full speed without any issues.
Of course, because even creatives still need to write some things out, I tested the keyboard thoroughly as well. It's a comfortable keyboard, just as I expected from Lenovo. It's comfortable to use for days on end, hours each day, and you won't need a different laptop keyboard unless you want one purely for aesthetic or ergonomic purposes.
Lenovo Yoga Pro 7i: Final verdict
The question that we land on is: should you buy this laptop? If you want a more portable but powerful creator workstation that isn't difficult to carry around in a backpack, then yes, you probably should buy this. It does everything mobile photo and video editors will need it to do.
However, if you need the extra screen space afforded by the 9i, I can see why that'd make sense for many deskbound creatives.
Either way, either laptop is a spectacular buy if you're in the creative space and don't need a true 4K display, because the screen itself, with its color accuracy, visuals, and refresh rate, is absolutely gorgeous. You get the reliability and dependability of the Lenovo family, all in a machine designed for creators to do exactly that: create.

Cómo crear un mensaje personalizado para mamá con IA
Crear un mensaje personalizado para mamá con inteligencia artificial requiere dar instrucciones y cuidar la información compartida.
El primer paso es ingresar a una herramienta de IA, como ChatGPT, Meta AI, Grok o Claude, y pedir un mensaje de felicitación por el Día de la Madre. Conviene indicar si se busca un texto breve, emotivo, divertido, formal o pensado para una tarjeta, WhatsApp o una publicación.
Para que el resultado tenga un tono personal, se pueden mencionar algunos detalles de la madre: sus gustos, una costumbre familiar, una enseñanza que haya dejado o una cualidad que se quiera destacar.
No es necesario incluir datos privados, direcciones, documentos, contraseñas, problemas de salud ni información confidencial. La idea es aportar referencias afectivas para que la felicitación no parezca genérica.
Por último, hay que explicarle a la IA el enfoque deseado. Por ejemplo, se puede pedir que el mensaje transmita gratitud, humor, admiración o cercanía; que incluya un recuerdo compartido sin inventarlo; o que evite frases solemnes.
Después, hay que revisar el resultado, ajustar las palabras que no representen la relación y añadir una despedida. Así, la herramienta funciona como un punto de partida, mientras que el mensaje conserva una voz personal.

articles.title: This 4K bird feeder camera nails focus, but its video frame rates let it down
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro is a well-built, easy-to-live-with smart feeder that keeps itself charged and produces nicely detailed 4K footage of back yard birds. But a 15fps cap on 4K video, an ultra slow-motion mode that doesn’t appear to work properly, a cluttered app and AI-assisted species ID locked behind a subscription mean it falls slightly short of justifying its premium price.
Reasons to buy
- + Detailed 4K images with the right settings
- + Sturdy, rattle-free build and easy installation
- + Easily removable dual-chamber hopper
- + Solar roof keeps the battery topped up
Reasons to avoid
- - -Best software features require a subscription
- - 4K video capped at 15fps; 120fps mode doesn’t play back smoothly
- - Birds sometimes come closer than the minimum focus distance
- - Cluttered, confusing app
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: two-minute review
Smart bird feeders have quietly become one of the busiest corners of the camera world. Hang one in your yard, garden or on a balcony railing and it’ll snap and film every feathered visitor automatically, often identifing the species for you, too. We’ve tested plenty of them here at TechRadar — you’ll find the best in our guide to the best bird feeder cameras — and the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro is the latest to land in my garden.
If it looks familiar, that’s because it’s clearly a descendant of the Kiwibit Beako, which we tested last year. The headline upgrade is in the camera: Kiwibit says this is the first bird feeder camera to combine 4K HDR with phase-detection autofocus (PDAF), the kind of focusing tech you’ll find in a decent smartphone. The other big change is a roof with solar panels built into it, so there’s no separate panel to mount and wire up.
That roof turns out to be one of the feeder’s best features. After an initial charge I never needed to plug it in again during testing, and the battery hovered near full. The rest of the hardware impresses too: the plastic shell is tough and well finished, mounting it took minutes, and lifting out the two-chamber seed hopper for a refill or clean is about as easy as it gets.
The camera is a game of two halves, though. Photos and 4K clips are crisp, and the autofocus generally locks on to birds reliably — though ones that hop right into the seed tray can get too close for it focus. The biggest frustration is motion: 4K is limited to 15 frames per second, which makes footage look juddery, and the 120fps slow-motion mode currently produces clips that are little better than slideshows. The 1080p 60fps mode is the pick of the bunch.
Then there’s the app, which is cluttered and hard to navigate, and keeps its most compelling feature — AI species identification — behind a Kiwibit Plus subscription. That ID system was accurate in my testing, even if it can only name one species per clip. Taken as a whole, the Bird Feeder 2 Pro’s hardware is impressive, but its software and video modes need to catch up.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: price and availability
- $279.99 in the US with 'lifetime AI' included, or $219.99 without
- £289.99 in the UK; launching Q1 2027
- Kiwibit Plus subscription priced from $7.99 per month
The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro is currently on sale in the US for $219.99, or $279.99 with a lifetime subscription to the Kiwibit Plus service. It’s due to arrive in the UK in the first quarter of 2027, priced at £289.99.
That price puts it in premium territory, alongside the likes of the Bird Buddy 2. And there’s a running cost to factor in, because AI species identification and several other app features require a Kiwibit Plus subscription, which costs from $89.99 (a UK price is TBC) per year or $7.99 a month.

| Dimensions | 9.8 x 8.7 x 8.9 inches / 25 x 22 x 22.7cm | 
| Weight | 4.08lbs / 1.85kg | 
| Connectivity | USB-C, Dual-band Wi-Fi 6 | 
| Battery | 5,200mAh battery, 5W solar panel | 
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: design
- Solar panels built into the hinged roof
- Removable 1.7l dual-compartment hopper
- IP65 rated and works in -4F to 122F (-20C to 50C) temperature range
Side by side with the Kiwibit Beako, the Bird Feeder 2 Pro is almost a dead ringer. The one key difference is up on top, with the solar panels now built into the roof. It’s a smart move that cuts down on clutter, as you don’t need to find somewhere else to mount a panel or route a cable.
The same roof also hides one of the feeder’s best design touches. Flip it up (it just requires you to press a button to release a latch) and you can lift the seed hopper straight out to clean or refill it. That hopper has two compartments, so you can offer two different seed mixes if you like, and each one has its own sliding door for shutting off the supply.
The body is almost entirely plastic, which won’t appeal to everyone. There are wooden and metal bird feeder cameras out there, and personally I’d prefer either material on something that lives in my garden. I also wonder whether the green plastic will fade in the sun over time, although I didn’t notice any change in my few weeks of testing.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
On the plus side, this is solid, hard-wearing plastic, and the feeder feels sturdier than others I’ve reviewed — the hinged roof, for instance, opens and closes without a hint of rattle. It’s IP65 rated and Kiwibit says it’ll work in temperatures from -4F to 122F (-20C to 50C), so bad weather shouldn’t be a worry for the electronics inside.
My review sample came with three mounting options: a fabric strap for wrapping around a tree or lamppost, a pole mount for stick it on the top of poles up to one inch (25.4mm) in diameter, and a wall bracket. I used the bracket to fix the feeder to a trellis against the back wall of my courtyard garden, and it took no time at all. A positioning sticker in the box shows you where to drill two guide holes, then two screws (also supplied) hold the bracket in place. There are wall plugs in the box too, should you need them.
The feeder itself attaches to the bracket with four small hex screws, and the same screws secure the perch. An Allen key is included in the box, but make sure you keep it somewhere safe or have a spare, as you’ll be in a pickle without one. My sample also came with a water beaker that clips on to the perch.
Power comes from a rechargeable, removable battery that’s topped up by the solar roof panels, and the combination works very well. I fully charged the battery via USB-C before installation, as the manual instructs, and haven’t charged it manually since — weeks later, it’s still sitting at 99% capacity. To be fair, my testing took place in a sunny late summer and early autumn, and I positioned the feeder to catch a few hours of direct sun each day. I’m curious to see how it copes with the gloomier winter months here in southeast England.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: performance
- 4K video capped at 15fps
- AI species ID requires a Kiwibit Plus subscription
- Phase-detection autofocus with a 130-degree view
Some bird feeder cameras I’ve tested have struggled to stay connected to my home Wi-Fi, but the Bird Feeder 2 Pro’s dual-band connection was stable throughout, even though the signal was rarely at full strength. The live feed kicked in from my phone without much delay, whenever I requested it.
Everything runs through Kiwibit’s app, and frankly it isn’t very well designed. There are too many sections with vague names, I regularly forgot where things lived, and getting to my photos and videos took more taps than it should. A simpler, pared-back layout would make a big difference.
There are some nice touches, mind you. Each species gets a written description, the Nature Expert section answers your bird questions, and the Collection page gives you a quick rundown of every species your camera has spotted. The catch is that many of the best features — especially the AI species identification, which feels like a core reason to buy this feeder — sit behind a Kiwibit Plus subscription. Kiwibit gave me a code for a year’s access, but for everyone else it’s an extra $89.99 on top of an already premium price, and the feeder feels noticeably less capable without it.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The identification itself was largely accurate. Only five species visited during my testing period, and the feeder correctly named four of them. That one miss was interesting, though: in a clip featuring a robin, a sparrow and a blue tit, only the robin was identified. That was the only clip containing a blue tit, so it appears the system tags just the first species it spots in each video. I’ve no doubt it would have recognized the blue tit on its own, but it’s a shame it can’t log multiple species in one clip.
Image quality is a more complicated story. 4K videos and photos generally look good, with plenty of sharpness and clarity, and the autofocus is accurate. There's even a microphone to capture sound, and it's nice to hear the birds chomping away on seeds or tweeting at each other. But 4K video is capped at just 15fps, which I found baffling. It makes clips look jerky, and it put me off using the 4K mode altogether. Why couldn't it just be 24fps or 30fps?
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Shooting in 4K does have one perk: the software may automatically pull a 12MP Ultra HD “Keyshot” still from your footage. These are sharpened and upscaled for extra detail, but I found them a little over-sharpened, and they’re oddly large files at around 10MB each, given the modest resolution. You can’t pick the frame yourself, either — the software chooses for you, and it doesn’t always choose well. There’s a second type of auto photo, called SwiftShot, which is generated in Ultra Slow Motion mode and is meant to freeze birds in flight. That never happened for me; every SwiftShot I got showed a bird sitting on the feeder, and in noticeable less detail than with the Ultra HD Keyshots.
Video clips are 10 seconds long by default, but extendable to three minutes. I’d have liked to catch birds flying in more often, but my videos generally started with the visitor already perched.
There are two slow-motion modes, both 1080p: 60fps and 120fps. The 120fps mode doesn’t appear to work properly at the time of writing. Whatever settings I tried, the footage seemed to be captured at 15fps, so it plays back like a slideshow when slowed down. I was expecting something akin to the iPhone's buttery-smooth slow-motion mode, but this is in the single digits frames-per-second wise. I’ve reported this to Kiwibit and I hope a firmware update fixes it, because for now it’s useless as a video mode. It may be intended mainly for grabbing crisp stills of birds in motion, but since you can’t choose the frame yourself and have to rely on Kiwibit’s cloud processing to pick it, that’s not much consolation.
The 60fps mode is far better. Played back at half speed you get smooth 30fps slow motion, or at quarter speed you get the same 15fps as the 4K clips. It lacks the fine detail of 4K, but its smoothness at normal and half speed makes it the sweet spot of the lineup for me. One quirk to note: neither slow-motion mode records sound, even when you play clips back at normal speed.
Autofocus is generally reliable, but birds that came right into the seed tray, rather than staying on the perch, were sometimes out of focus. They seem to be inside the minimum focus distance, which was also an issue with the Beako. It’s not a huge deal, but it’s annoying when a bird’s body is sharp and its eyes and beak are soft.
Sharing and saving photos and videos is easy – you just hit the share button when viewing in the app and you get the option to download the file to your phone, or share via a variety of means. Subscribers also get cloud storage for all their files.
Should you buy the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro?
Buy it if...
You want detailed 4K stills
Its 4K photos are sharp and clear, and the phase-detection autofocus is accurate.
You never want to charge a battery
The solar roof kept the battery near full for weeks without me plugging it in once.
You want easy upkeep
The removable two-chamber hopper makes refilling and cleaning quick and lets you offer two seed mixes.
Don't buy it if...
You want smooth video
4K is capped at 15fps, and the 120fps slow-motion mode currently plays back like a slideshow.
You don’t want a subscription
AI species identification, a key selling point, is locked behind Kiwibit Plus.
You’d prefer a natural-looking feeder
It’s almost entirely plastic, so look elsewhere if you’d rather have wood or metal in your garden.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: also consider
Bird Buddy 2
Priced at around $299 / £300, the Bird Buddy 2 also has a solar roof, and its app is far more polished and enjoyable to use, with free AI species ID. Its standard video is only at 1080p resolution, though, with 2K reserved for subscribers.
Read our Bird Buddy 2 review
Camouflage EZ BirdFeed
If you’re in Europe and value matters more than image quality, this £139 feeder is hard to beat. It offers AI bird ID with no subscription and twin roof-mounted solar panels, but its 1080p images can’t match the Kiwibit’s crisp detail.
Read our Camouflage EZ BirdFeed review
How I tested the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro
- Mounted on a garden trellis for several weeks in late summer/early fall
- Tested all video modes, including both slow-motion settings
- Used the app with a Kiwibit Plus subscription
I installed the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro in my garden in southeast England using the supplied wall bracket, fixing it to a trellis in a spot that got a few hours of direct sunlight a day. After fully charging the battery via USB, I left it to run on solar power for the rest of the testing period, which ran through late summer into early autumn.
I tested the feeder with the Kiwibit app on my phone, using a year’s Kiwibit Plus subscription supplied by Kiwibit to access the AI species ID and other premium features. I tried every video mode, including 4K and both 1080p slow-motion settings, compared the automatically generated KeyShot and SwiftShot stills, and checked the AI identifications against the birds I could see in each clip.
- First reviewed October 2026
Sam has been writing about tech and digital culture for over 20 years, starting off in video games journalism before branching out into the wonderful worlds of consumer electronics, streaming entertainment and photography. Over the years he has written for Wired, Stuff, GQ, T3, Trusted Reviews and PC Zone, and now lives on the Kent coast in the UK – the ideal place for a camera reviewer to ply their trade.

articles.title: L'ID. Buzz aura droit à une deuxième génération et Volkswagen veut corriger son principal défaut
articles.text:
Thomas Schäfer, patron de Volkswagen, a confirmé qu’une deuxième génération de l’ID. Buzz était en préparation, à l’occasion du Mondial de l’Auto de Paris. Pour la vendre moins cher, le constructeur compte sur sa future plateforme SSP et sur des batteries plus économiques.
Plus de 10 000 clients attendaient la livraison de leur ID. Buzz début 2023 et l’usine Volkswagen de Hanovre avait produit 10 800 exemplaires du Combi électrique en moins d’un an. Près de quatre ans plus tard, le constructeur déchante et a bien du mal à écouler son van. Aux États-Unis, Volkswagen a vendu seulement 432 ID. Buzz au troisième trimestre 2026, contre 2 469 un an plus tôt, selon les ventes trimestrielles relevées par CarBuzz. Le groupe sait que les acheteurs reculent devant le prix. Pour proposer un successeur moins cher, il attend une nouvelle plateforme, et celle-ci a environ trois ans de retard sur le plan de départ.
Des batteries LFP pour alléger la facture de l’ID. Buzz
« L’ID. Buzz repose sur une mauvaise base de coûts. Il lui est donc difficile de vraiment réussir et de se vendre en volume, malheureusement », a expliqué Thomas Schäfer lors d’un entretien sur l’avenir du van accordé au magazine britannique Auto Express. En France, Volkswagen vend son Combi électrique à partir de 49 540 euros en cinq places et à partir de 59 350 euros en sept places, d’après son configurateur en ligne. Si vous avez besoin des sept places pour une famille nombreuse, vous devez donc prévoir plus de 59 000 euros avant la moindre option.
Thomas Schäfer a évoqué les batteries lithium-fer-phosphate (LFP) pour faire baisser la note du prochain modèle. Les fabricants produisent ces cellules sans nickel ni cobalt, et elles coûtent moins cher que les batteries NMC (nickel-manganèse-cobalt). Volkswagen a recours à cette chimie sur l’ID. Polo. Le constructeur équipe les versions d’entrée de gamme de sa citadine électrique, vendue moins de 25 000 euros, d’une batterie LFP de 37 kWh.
Le patron de Volkswagen défend malgré tout le pari du Combi et de son style rétro. « Il montre que si l’on reste fidèle à la marque, on peut avoir une marque enthousiasmante », a-t-il ajouté.
Le futur ID. Buzz attendra la plateforme SSP
Volkswagen construira la deuxième génération du van sur la SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), à la place de la plateforme MEB de l’actuel ID. Buzz. Toutes les marques du groupe utiliseront cette architecture pour leurs futurs modèles électriques, et Thomas Schäfer compte sur ces volumes pour réduire les coûts de développement et de production. Les conducteurs gagneront aussi en autonomie et en vitesse de recharge, d’après Auto Express.
Herbert Diess, alors patron du groupe Volkswagen, avait présenté la SSP en juillet 2021 et promis un premier modèle pour 2026. Aucune voiture de série n’est encore produite sur cette plateforme aujourd’hui. Gernot Döllner, patron d’Audi, a repoussé à mars 2029 au plus tôt la production de l’A4 e-tron, attendue pour inaugurer la SSP. Motor1 relie ce retard à une décision de Volkswagen, prise en plein développement, de remplacer le réseau de bord en 12 volts par un circuit en 48 volts.
Le premier modèle SSP de la marque Volkswagen sera un grand SUV attendu avant la fin de la décennie, et le nouvel ID. Buzz arrivera après lui, affirme Auto Express. Le prochain Combi électrique devrait donc arriver après 2030, estime Automobile Propre. Volkswagen prépare d’ici là des mises à jour du modèle actuel.
Andreas Mindt, chef du design de Volkswagen, garde en tête la leçon de la New Beetle pour dessiner le prochain van. « On fait une Beetle, puis une autre, et les gens finissent par se lasser », a-t-il confié à Auto Express, avant de promettre un ID. Buzz « intéressant ».

articles.title: Nos sextoys ne remplacent pas les hommes, mais révèlent ce qu’ils refusent de voir
articles.text:
Nos sextoys ne remplacent pas les hommes, mais révèlent ce qu’ils refusent de voir
Lettre ouverte aux mâles qui se sentent menacés
Et si le vrai rival des hommes n’était pas un autre homme, mais un petit objet en silicone ? Holà, fiers gaillards : loin d’être une menace, le sextoy interroge notre rapport féminin au plaisir, à la virilité et à la place du partenaire. Il ne remplace pas, que nenni, il complète ! À condition, bien sûr, de le juger autrement.
Cet article répond aux nombreuses réactions que nous avons reçues sur nos réseaux et forums sur les sextoys féminins. Il propose un regard différent sur la façon dont certains hommes perçoivent l’évolution de la sexualité féminine. Rien ici n’a vocation à choquer ou braquer qui que ce soit : le but est simplement d’observer, comprendre… et dédramatiser.
Messieurs,
Je vais vous parler d’un appareil que vous considérez comme un redoutable compétiteur. Un concurrent silencieux, compact, souvent de couleur rose pastel. Il ne parle pas, ne drague pas, ne sort pas les poubelles. Et pourtant, il déclenche chez certains d’entre vous des crises de jalousie d’une intensité rare. Oui, il s'agit bel et bien du sextoy, du stimulateur clitoridien, du vibromasseur qui, paraît-il, ruinerait votre virilité.
Depuis quelque temps, sur nos réseaux et forums comme dans certaines discussions privées, on entend sortir de vos bouches des plaintes à peine voilées : “Ma femme, je la satisfais, elle n’a pas à chercher ailleurs.” “La mienne n'a plus besoin de moi si c'est pour qu'elle me préfère son jouet.”
C’est fascinant, cette peur viscérale qu’un petit appareil en silicone puisse vous détrôner. Comme si l’idée même qu’une femme explore parfois seule son plaisir était une menace, une remise en cause de votre utilité, voire de votre place dans le lit conjugal.
Alors rassurez-vous, un sextoy n’a pas pour mission de vous remplacer. Il ne fera jamais un bon café le matin à votre partenaire, il ne partagera pas avec elle un fou rire, il ne lui caressera pas une épaule au bon moment. Surtout, le jouet sexuel ne regardera pas votre partenaire avec désir. Ce qu’il fait, c’est vibrer, ni plus ni moins. Et ça, aucun homme, aussi motivé soit-il, n’est capable de le reproduire. C'est ainsi, il faut l'accepter.
Lelo Sona 2
Womanizer Premium 2
Croyez-moi, les sextoys ne sont pas vos vils adversaires, ce sont même vos alliés, car ils ne diminuent pas la place du partenaire, ils élargissent le champ des possibles. Ils rappellent surtout une vérité fondamentale que trop d’hommes oublient : le plaisir féminin n’est pas une récompense ni un indicateur de performance, mais un territoire à partager, à encourager, à laisser s’exprimer librement, même (et surtout) en dehors de vous.
L’idée qu’une femme puisse se donner du plaisir en mode solitaire, sans en référer à son compagnon, semble encore insupportable à certains. Parce que ça ébranle (sic) l’ego, ça déplace le centre du monde. Mais une femme épanouie, c’est aussi une femme qui sait ce qu’elle aime, qui connaît son corps et n’attend pas qu’on le découvre à sa place. Une femme qui se fait du bien seule ne s’éloigne pas de vous ; elle se rapproche d’elle-même. Et croyez-moi, c’est plutôt une bonne nouvelle pour tout le monde.
Dans les laboratoires des Numériques, nous testons les stimulateurs clitoridiens comme nous testons les smartphones, les montres ou les aspirateurs, c'est-à-dire avec sérieux, méthode et curiosité. Parce qu’il s’agit d’un produit technologique comme un autre, pensé pour améliorer le bien-être. Et pourtant, c’est encore le seul objet dont l’efficacité semble déranger certains hommes. Dites, les gars, un casque audio à réduction du bruit ne vous rend pas soupçonneux. Un aspirateur-balai qui nettoie mieux que vous ne vous fait pas douter de vos aptitudes. Alors pourquoi un sextoy ? Peut-être parce que dans cette histoire, le plaisir n’est plus centré sur vous. Eh bien, si c’était justement ça, le progrès ?
Alors Messieurs, plutôt que de vous sentir menacés, soyez curieux, intéressez-vous, parlez-en. Intégrez ces jouets dans le jeu au lieu de les vivre comme des intrus. Le plaisir féminin ne vous exclut pas, il vous invite à participer autrement, écouter davantage, déconstruire ce que la culture ancestrale de la virilité a pu vous faire croire sur la sexualité.
Une femme heureuse, détendue, comblée — que ce soit grâce à vous, un sextoy, ou une combinaison des deux —, c’est une femme qui a envie. De vous, entre autres. Alors, au lieu de vous défier du silicone, vous devriez peut-être lui dire merci.

articles.title: ServiceNow AI Control Tower: Selling a penthouse while building the frame - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
ServiceNow AI Control Tower: Selling a penthouse while building the frame
ServiceNow Inc. is making one of the more consequential and visible bets in enterprise artificial intelligence. The company says AI Control Tower can discover and govern any agent, work across models and clouds, track cost and value, and shut down behavior that violates policy.
That sales pitch plays directly to ServiceNow’s greatest asset – its installed base. Information technology and service management or ITSM, configuration management database or CMDB, risk workflows, security operations and years of operating context give the company a distribution and data advantage most AI and governance vendors do not have.
Our research suggests that moat is real. But proprietary customer data shows a more nuanced picture. Control Tower is already strong as a governance workflow and system of action. It can inventory AI assets, connect risks to owners, route approvals and remediation, and preserve an audit trail. What the field study has not broadly validated is the claim that Control Tower is a complete technical governance and runtime enforcement plane across the heterogeneous enterprise.
In this Breaking Analysis episode, we use a methodology similar to our CoreWeave analysis, and pressure-test management’s statements against 15 in-depth interviews with ServiceNow customers conducted with our data partner, Qualitate. We ask the following question: Is Control Tower becoming the enterprise AI control plane – or is it limited to the governance system of action?
Access the full slide deck here with survey data in the appendix.
Three distinct technical jobs – ServiceNow dominates only one today
ServiceNow may not need to own every technical control to build a very large business bolstered by AI governance. It can create enormous value by owning the workflow around those controls – inventory, accountability, approvals, exceptions, remediation and audit history.
But its marketing pitch is allowing customers to think the the market is collapsing three jobs into one convenient phrase: AI governance.
The first is governance workflow and accountability. This is where ServiceNow is strongest.
The second is AI lifecycle evidence – model versions, lineage, validation, bias, explainability and drift. ServiceNow can coordinate that evidence, but customers often generate it elsewhere.
The third is runtime enforcement and AI security – intercepting an action, blocking a deployment, constraining an agent or revoking access in real time. Our survey indicates this layer is frequently external, custom or human.
The nuance is that approving a model and assigning a remediation ticket are valuable. But they are not the same as technically validating the model, proving lineage or blocking the action.
ServiceNow’s opportunity is to connect all three. It is not best-of-breed in each today according to its own customers. Broadly, buyers should be cautious of claims that ServiceNow AI Control Tower is a platform that is universally end-to-end.
The five pillars of ServiceNow’s AI strategy
Control Tower sits inside a broader ServiceNow agentic AI strategy built on five connected pillars as shown below.
First is a model-agnostic posture: Any model, agent, cloud, data source or system of record.
Second is the shift from chat assistants to autonomous workers that plan, execute and adapt across workflows.
Third is centralized governance through AI Control Tower – discovery, ownership, access, observability, value and remediation.
Fourth is AI cost and value management: Token economics, model selection, budget control and ROI.
Fifth is pricing and packaging. Foundation, Advanced and Prime tiers seed AI broadly, move customers up the stack and add consumption on top of subscriptions.
These pillars reinforce one another and describe ServiceNow’s advantage and momentum. More agents create more governance demand. Model choice creates complexity. Governance addresses complexity and creates more reasons to stay on the platform. And more usage drives more consumption.
Our focus today is the key link in that flywheel chain: Can AI Control Tower can extend ServiceNow’s workflow advantage into technical governance and runtime control?
The numbers underscore ServiceNow’s AI momentum
Management’s “right-to-win” argument is not that ServiceNow builds the best foundation models. It is that ServiceNow already knows how work moves through the enterprise.
Bill McDermott describes the moat in one word: context.
ServiceNow says its platform supports roughly 100 billion workflows and nearly 8 trillion transactions. Amit Zavery said more than 500 customers were live with AI Control Tower in the first six months. And ServiceNow reported AI ACV above 1 billion dollars in Q2, with a full-year target of $1.5 billion.
The CMDB knows assets, services, owners and dependencies. ITSM and change management know how work is routed and approved. IRM understands controls, risks, issues and evidence.
A best-of-breed specialist will likely have deeper model analytics, but it often lacks the operational graph that identifies the owner, business service or the path to remediate an issue.
The installed base gives ServiceNow a right to compete. It does not, by itself, prove that every technical control is present or every runtime path is governed.
Field study of 15 ServiceNow customers
A quick word on methodology.
TheCUBE Research commissioned a study through its partner, Qualitate, which conducted the fieldwork from Sept. 15-21, 2026.
The final base is 15 completed large-enterprise interviews totaling 575 minutes. Eleven respondents were in North America and four in Europe. Five came from financial services, four from healthcare, three from technology and telecommunications, and three from public sector, manufacturing or other industries.
The sample was senior: three executives or vice presidents, 10 directors or functional heads, and two senior managers.
Every respondent had an existing ServiceNow footprint. The study is a deliberate qualitative study of expansion, coexistence, implementation and control boundaries inside real accounts. Eleven of the 15 customers had either installed, piloted or were actively evaluating ServiceNow AI Control Tower.
There’s of course a bias toward the ServiceNow installed base. That is by design and it’s useful because management’s premise is it has an installed-base premise. We are testing the environment where Control Tower should have its greatest advantage.
Our methodology specifically separates direct experience from management claims. This is not a survey with 15 customers supplied by ServiceNow.
ServiceNow is building on its workflow and operational moat
This next chart speaks to the heart of the episode.
All 15 respondents recognized ServiceNow’s workflow, operational integration or incumbency advantage.
Fourteen of 15, however described runtime enforcement as external, custom, human mediated, limited to selected paths or not proven at enterprise scale. The one exception was a limited financial-services pilot that successfully tested ServiceNow’s blocking capability for at least one model and one agent.
Twelve of 15 identified a model-specific evidence gap – validation records, lineage, bias, explainability, drift history or AI-specific regulatory artifacts.
And twelve of 15 tied governance value or switching cost to the wider Now Platform – mainly ITSM, CMDB, change management and SecOps.
Our research shows that the same ServiceNow architecture creates both the moat and the boundary limits. Specifically, ServiceNow is hard to displace because governance work is embedded in operations. But the value story degrades when the CMDB is immature, the AI estate sits outside ServiceNow control paths, or regulators require technical evidence generated elsewhere.
One respondent called ServiceNow more like a governance orchestration layer than the actual governance of AI. We would challenge that a bit: It is real governance, but strongest at orchestrating accountability and action.
Regarding CMDB – when we first started covering ServiceNow in 2013, ServiceNow management would constantly push customers to consolidate on a single CMDB, which today is the norm. This has given ServiceNow a tremendous incumbency advantage but customers encounter friction.
A senior engineering manager at a large North American financial services company summed it up like this:
The CMDB dependency is bigtime on this because it must be cleaned up quite often, and that is the reason there are a lot of surveys that have been sent within the organization to actually clean up the CMDB on a regular basis. And a lot of auditing around is to be done as part of that.
Unpacking the three fundamental operating layers of AI governance
The interviews suggest that AI governance is separating into three operating layers, with different buyers and budgets as shown below.
The first is governance workflow and accountability: Here we mean inventory, ownership, approvals, exceptions, issues, remediation and audit history. ServiceNow has the clearest advantage here.
The second is AI lifecycle evidence and regulatory proof: We’re talking about functions like model versions, lineage, validation, bias, explainability, drift and performance history. Hyperscaler-native tools, model platforms and specialists often supply this layer. Players here include IBM with Watsonx.governance, Fiddler AI; or a company like Credo AI which is strong at regulatory mapping and audit trail.
The third is runtime enforcement and AI security: Gateway policies, permission checks, agent identity, deployment gates and the ability to block or constrain actions. Security and AI platform budgets usually fund it. Palo Alto Prisma AIRS and Cisco AI Defense are good examples here.
This explains why architectures remain multi-vendor even when vendors claim end-to-end governance. There are three different activities involved including:
- The completion of a workflow;
- A model validation artifact – for example, a report generated while evaluating a model to prove how well it works; and
- A blocked action at runtime – versus an asynchronous alert to a human.
The question for ServiceNow is can it own every layer? Or will it become the policy authority and hub for evidence that connects these three layers and acts as the system of action?
This is where the field study we did with Qualitate strongly validates management’s story and at the same time highlights some notable weaknesses.
ServiceNow’s differentiation: Turning a governance finding into actual work
An AI asset can be connected to an application, business service, owner and dependency in the CMDB. IRM can attach controls, risks, issues, evidence and exceptions. ITSM, change management and Action Fabric can route the finding, track remediation and preserve the audit history.
Note: Action Fabric is ServiceNow’s interoperability and governance framework that lets external AI agents like Claude execute multistep workflows inside ServiceNow in a headless manner — similar to the way we reported on Salesforce’s Headless 360 – bypassing the traditional interface.
One respondent put it like this: Day one ServiceNow, day one workflow. Another said the CMDB matters because an AI risk can be connected to the application and business-service owner.
That is important because model-risk tool may detect drift or bias, but if the organization cannot assign, prioritize, remediate and prove what happened, the control has limited operational value.
This is why “just ticketing” is the wrong criticism. Operational accountability is part of governance.
The more accurate description in our view is that ServiceNow is exceptionally well-positioned to be the system of action for AI governance. The question is how much technical evidence and enforcement it can bring into that system.
What an end-to-end architecture should deliver
This next diagram shows what actually flows when the architecture works as advertised.
AI Control Tower discovers the asset and establishes ownership. The CMDB supplies application, service and dependency context. IRM brings policy, risk, control, evidence and exception records. ITSM and Action Fabric turn the finding into assigned remediation work.
That internal path is ServiceNow’s sweet spot.
The limits show up when the organization needs technical model evidence or a live intervention at runtime. The technical validation may come from a model platform or specialist vendor. Blocking may occur in an application programming interface gateway or security product. The telemetry then has to return to Control Tower as evidence.
In several of our customer interviews, that connection was incomplete or fuzzy. Different teams owned governance, model tooling and security. Data models and workflows did not align automatically.
ServiceNow does not have to be the box that blocks every action. But it should define policy, identify the owner, send the decision to the right enforcement point, receive telemetry and preserve the audit trail.
That’s the closed loop.
Caveat emptor of ‘kill switch’ claims
Bill McDermott stated on CNBC’s “Mad Money” in July 2026, that ServiceNow possesses a kill switch to halt rogue AI agents and prevent disruptions, contrasting it with incidents like OpenAI’s agent escaping a test environment and hacking Hugging Face.
Buyer beware on this claim. Our survey exposes the limitations of this assertion.
Only one respondent reported a very positive pilot and that was limited. In this case, at least one model and one agent were tested for blocking, auditors were satisfied, and the respondent gave high marks. So that case directly supports management’s claim in a selected environment.
But the other 14 respondents described runtime control as external, custom, human mediated, limited to selected paths or not proven at scale.
What has not been validated – and appears to be a gap – is universal coverage across Azure OpenAI, custom agents, SaaS copilots, third-party models, shadow AI, multiple clouds and non-ServiceNow workflows.
One security practitioner estimated that only 30% to 40% of total AI activity could realistically pass through ServiceNow control paths today.
Our assessment is the kill-switch claim is overstated. It is not yet proven as a universal enterprise runtime control plane.
Unpacking procedural vs. technical evidence
ServiceNow is strong at procedural proof – showing who approved a use case, which control was completed, who owns the exception, whether remediation occurred and what the audit history looks like. Several respondents said auditors accepted the ServiceNow record.
The gaps become more obvious in high-risk or regulated use cases. Survey respondents indicated ServiceNow gaps in many areas related to what we’re calling technical proof, including: Validation methodology, test dataset, model versions, training-data lineage, bias and fairness results, explainability, drift and performance history, prompt and response evaluations, hallucination and toxicity tests, permission evidence and a record of what the agent did at runtime.
Those artifacts are most often generated by alternative platforms – for example. IBM, hyperscaler-native governance tooling, other model platforms, MLOps systems, privacy and AI governance specialists, or traditional model-risk tools.
Control Tower can still become the place where that evidence is captured, evaluated, linked to policy and operationalized. But ServiceNow is currently out over its skis in our view, using “end-to-end” language. Our survey data suggests that, today anyway, ServiceNow is weaker at showing the complete evidence path for a real model or agent across a heterogeneous environment.
Buying decisions are heavily influenced by ServiceNow footprint and risk
Buying indicators become clearer when we assess two variables: ServiceNow footprint depth and the intensity of AI or model risk. The four quadrants below explain this dynamic in simple terms.
Where ServiceNow is deeply embedded and regulation is modest, Control Tower has its best expansion opportunity – the lower right on this chart. This is the consolidation sweet spot for ServiceNow and probably represents the largest total available market.
The upper right shows where regulation is high and ServiceNow is deep, customers often preserve ServiceNow as the system of action but add independent lifecycle evidence and runtime controls. Coexistence is likely. That’s also a fairly large chunk of the market.
Where regulation is high and the ServiceNow footprint is shallow, the field is open to independent AI governance and model-risk tools. That is shown on the upper left.
Where both are limited, hyperscaler-native controls or lighter specialists may be good enough – lower left.
Our analysis also exposes three different buyer-personas.
- IT operations and platform owners value workflow, context and consolidation;
- Model risk and AI governance teams value technical proof;
- Security teams own runtime control.
The vendor that speaks to only one persona may win the feature argument and still lose the account.
A new pricing and packaging model for AI
ServiceNow’s commercial strategy is worth exploring. This spring, ahead of ServiceNow Knowledge, the company replaced its legacy package tiers (Standard, Professional, Enterprise, Pro Plus and Enterprise Plus) with three AI-native pricing and packaging tiers: Foundation, Advanced and Prime.
Foundation, Advanced and Prime give customers an upgrade path, but some customers bristle. Management reports price uplifts of roughly 20% to 30% in the lower AI tiers and more than 30% in Prime, with subscription commitments paired with usage-based meters.
Our survey supports the momentum in ServiceNow ACVs. It shows that the operating model drives higher invoices. But the data also exposes some meaningful customer friction.
Twelve of 15 respondents said pricing, packaging or total-cost were acute concerns. Thirteen described significant configuration, integration or staffing friction.
As shown above, eight respondents supplied actual data comparing expectations to actual costs. Seven of the eight said costs came in above expectations, and one described the rollout as broadly on budget.
The cost overruns were not from licensing issues alone. They included partners, data normalization, CMDB hygiene, custom workflows, integration engineering, permanent specialists, administration and external controls.
One respondent said: We expected to need ServiceNow specialists, but we underestimated how permanent that would be.
Some verbatim quotes from the customers regarding pricing:
“ServiceNow is expensive”
“the packaging is frustrating”
“We expect costs to increase”
“the proposed quote is too high”
“Our costs came in 30% above our original expectation”
Importantly, this does not mean the value is poor. Some customers justified the extra cost. The issue is predictability. Customers should force ServiceNow to sell a bounded outcome, make integration assumptions explicit and show the full operating cost.
The market is showing distinct budget opportunities
The broader market is fragmenting into different budget layers as shown below. Control Tower touches them all but ServiceNow faces credible competition in each.
Runtime enforcement and AI security include Palo Alto Networks, Guardrails AI, Kong, Lakera, HiddenLayer and Protect AI.
Hyperscaler-native governance includes Microsoft Purview and Azure AI, Bedrock Guardrails and Vertex AI governance.
Specialist or AI governance leaders include IBM, OneTrust, Credo AI, Holistic AI and ModelOp. Traditional GRC and model-risk tools include Archer, AuditBoard, MetricStream, LogicGate and Navex.
Notably, 12 of fifteen respondents were evaluating or deploying separate runtime controls, usually from cybersecurity or AI platform budgets.
The obvious opportunity for ServiceNow is to orchestrate and preserve evidence across all these tools. The risk is that the vendor owning the enforcement point also captures the telemetry, the security buyer and eventually the policy decision. ServiceNow could receive a ticket after the fact instead of controlling the loop.
The answer is potentially openness with authority: Customers choose any enforcement technology while Control Tower remains the policy system, accountability layer and durable evidence system of record to support the overall system of action.
Pressure testing ServiceNow management’s claims
This scorecard below summarizes our test.
The incumbency and context moat is most definitely supported by our survey. All fifteen respondents recognized ServiceNow’s workflow, operational or installed-base advantage.
Model-agnostic orchestration is directionally supported. Customers value broad connectivity, but connector breadth is not the same as control depth.
The end-to-end governance claim is a stretch in our view. Control Tower is strong on inventory, accountability and procedural evidence but model-specific artifacts are frequently generated elsewhere.
The kill-switch claim is also overstated in our view. It is supported for selected pathways but definitely not yet as a universal runtime control plane. One positive pilot is good, but 14 respondents describing external, custom or limited enforcement suggest immaturity.
Execution watch: Cost transparency is an issue. Value management is a credible promise. The packaging creates attach and consumption opportunity but implementation remains a source of friction.
The field is most definitely not saying Control Tower is vaporware. Claims that it’s just a bolt-on are overstated; but its scope is currently limited.
The bottom line is ServiceNow is strongest where governance turns into actual work. It is less proven where governance becomes mathematical model evidence or a real-time intervention across a heterogeneous estate.
The investor angle points to a strong bull case with gaps to fill
From an investor and strategic perspective, the bull case is compelling.
AI Control Tower creates a new attach point into a sticky and powerful installed base. It converts CMDB context into a governance system of action. The model-agnostic posture gives optionality across labs and hyperscalers. And the commercial model creates subscription uplift plus consumption.
But there are areas of concern that we describe below.
Based on our customer surveys, runtime claims are ahead of broad field validation. Model-specific evidence still depends on adjacent tools with better depth. Implementation friction can slow adoption and create cost overrun surprises. Security vendors, deep governance experts and hyperscalers can capture control points and budget.
We believe the business can be excellent without ServiceNow owning every technical control. Orchestration is the strongest position because buyers rarely want to replace every model platform, security product or cloud control. They want a common policy, accountability and action layer.
The company’s valuation has fluctuated substantially peaking in late 2024 at around $230 billion dipping to the mid-$80 billion range in April of this year. It’s market cap is now on the rise again at around $146 billion as of this writing. The market cap debate will rest on how successfully ServiceNow can convince investors that it’s an AI winner; which in part, will depend on the company’s ability to monetize the closed loop we described earlier.
If Control Tower becomes the policy authority and evidence hub, the moat expands. If it only receives alerts after other products make the important decisions, the strategic value is more limited. Our bet is on the former because of the company’s footprint.
Customer action item: Make the closed loop prove itself before you scale
The research does not say Control Tower lacks value. Quite the opposite. Customers consistently value ServiceNow’s workflow, CMDB context, accountability and ability to turn a governance finding into work. But orchestration is not the same thing as technical enforcement, and that distinction is where buyers can get into trouble. In fourteen of the fifteen interviews, broad runtime enforcement was external, custom, human-mediated, limited to selected pathways or not yet proven at enterprise scale.
Start by mapping the control sequence. For one specific model or agent, name the policy owner, the source of model-level evidence, the exact enforcement point, the telemetry path and the remediation owner. Do not accept an architecture in which every arrow disappears into a black box control plane.
Next, test a real violation. Pick a high-risk use case – for example an agent that can access sensitive data, move money, change infrastructure or interact with customers. Trigger a policy breach and show where the action is blocked or constrained. Then verify that the event comes back into the governance record, creates the right case, assigns an owner and preserves the evidence an auditor would need and accept.
Third, price the full operating model – not just the Control Tower license. Include IRM and CMDB dependencies, data normalization, connectors, implementation partners, external runtime controls, AI uplifts, service fees and the recurring specialists needed to maintain the system. Our interviews show that those operating costs are where many programs moved significantly beyond their original expectations.
Finally, protect optionality. This is fundamental to your AI sovereignty. Architect around open APIs, explicit integration responsibilities, service levels and have compensating controls for an exit path. Buyers should have a shared accountability model with their vendors and internal stakeholders. Understand who owns the policy, who owns the enforcement point and who is accountable when a handoff fails.
The buyer gate should be no production-scale growth until one real violation is detected, blocked, recorded and remediated end to end. ServiceNow can be the system of action without being the only control. The buyer’s job is to prove that the entire system works as a system.
